summary: The entry as a whole has a credible research home. It settles, with a kernel-checked proof, a uniqueness question that Kulaichev raised in print in 1984, and Chiodo (C. R. Math. 2021) calls that question still open. The likely readers are specialists in the history and geometry of the Śrī Yantra and people working on certified computation and real algebraic geometry. The literature account is careful and precise: I checked the quotations, page references, DOIs and the self-citations, and they hold up. The golden-slope-product theorem uses a fourth condition the submitter chose, motivated only by the submitter's own non-peer-reviewed papers on solids. Its interest rests mainly on the 43/24 counts, which are not formalised, and the account says both things openly. One material gap: the account says no outside source asks for the golden condition, but it leaves out the earlier golden-ratio constructions of the Śrī Yantra (Bolton and Macleod; Fonseca) that Chiodo reviews in §1.2.2, one of its own main sources.

findings.evidence: Submission, 'The golden product: where it comes from'; Chiodo, C. R. Math. 359 (2021), §1.2.2 (p. 386 of the PDF; also the French summary)
findings.message: The account introduces a golden-ratio fourth condition (uv = 2/φ³) and says no outside source asks for it. It does not mention that golden-ratio constructions of the Śrī Yantra already exist. Chiodo, one of the entry's own main sources, reviews the straightedge-and-compass constructions 'based on the golden ratio' by Bolton and Macleod and by Fonseca (Religion 16, 1986), which 'fail to meet concurrency conditions in a way that is not visible to the eye'. He notes that golden-ratio and 'perfect construction' hypotheses keep circulating, and there are numerous attempts on the internet. A reader of the second theorem should know this history. Please add a short paragraph that cites these constructions and states how the exact condition here differs: it is imposed on top of Huet's exact concurrencies and Kulaichev's (b)–(d), it is not an approximate drawing method, and it makes no claim that the traditional makers used the golden ratio.

internal_notes.message: Both quotations match verbatim: 'il se pose la question (toujours ouverte) de l'unicité' and 'argues that the answer is out of reach. This problem is not considered here'. So a published question with a citable open status is established. This is the positive evidence behind the research-audience requirement for the entry as a whole.

internal_notes.message: The notability floor is carried mainly by kulaichev_unique and kulaichev_slope. They settle a 1984 question that a 2021 paper in a research journal calls open; the readers are historians of Indian mathematics, specialists in Śrī Yantra geometry (Huet, Chiodo, Rao, Pustynski), and people interested in certified interval and real-root methods. golden_unique and golden_slope do not raise notability. On their own they would be borderline: the condition is the submitter's own, motivated by non-peer-reviewed self-cited papers, and the feature that makes the figure interesting (traditional 43 triangles, 24 sandhis) is outside Lean. #103 Table 3 also lists other fourth conditions that give 43 triangles, so the golden condition does not uniquely single out the traditional form. The account discloses all this honestly. The added theorem does not manufacture its own advertised conclusion (uniqueness under a stated condition is a substantive claim), so it does not pull the entry below the floor.

Spot check of arithmetic. The regular icosahedron's face pyramid from the centre has lateral slope (face circumradius / inradius) = (2/√3)/(φ²/√3) = 2/φ² ≈ 0.7639, as stated. 2/φ³ = 2√5 − 4 ≈ 0.4721 is correct. The golden antiprism slope of 1/φ was not checked (the source is a self-cited Zenodo paper and was not read).

internal_notes.evidence: Rao 1998 (as quoted in submission); satyori.com summary
internal_notes.message: Rao's remark that 'an unlimited number of figures' meet the traditional specifications, and a popular-source report of a near-φ height ratio in Rao's solution, both confirm that golden-ratio claims about the Śrī Yantra circulate. This supports the finding above. The submission already discloses that the golden product is not the only condition giving the traditional counts.

golden_unique and golden_slope are planned, not built. As instructed, they were scored as if proved exactly as stated. The submission states this openly, and a Version 2 claim should not be registered until it is built.

I could not read Pustynski 2014 (the IJHS URL returned 404), the HAL copy of Chiodo (bot-blocked), Tahta 1992 (paywalled) or Kulaichev's Addition. The submission discloses its own unread items precisely. No finding rests on these.

The submission gives the Comparator configuration's theorem order (kulaichev_unique, kulaichev_slope, golden_unique, golden_slope) but not its definition list. Definitions are listed in Challenge-file source order.
No independent search contradicted the claim that no Śrī Yantra formalization exists outside the submitter's own Version 1 Palomar entry. Mathlib has none to my knowledge.

what_would_reach_higher: Add a paragraph that cites the earlier golden-ratio constructions of the Śrī Yantra (Bolton and Macleod; Fonseca, Religion 16 (1986) 33–49, both reviewed in Chiodo §1.2.2). State that those are approximate drawings that miss the concurrencies, that the condition here is exact and imposed on Huet's conditions plus Kulaichev's (b)–(d), and that no historical claim about the golden ratio is made.
Build and register golden_unique and golden_slope before claiming Version 2. As things stand, half the entry is a pilot with sorry.

Give the golden theorem a reason to matter that the formalisation itself carries: either formalise the 43-triangle / 24-sandhi count for both figures (a certified arrangement check in Lean would make the 'Kulaichev's figure is not traditional; the golden-product figure is' contrast part of the record), or present the second theorem only as a worked instance of the method.

Put the #103 Table 3 alternatives (other fourth conditions from solids that also give 43 triangles) in the Challenge header as well as the description, so the Lean-side account does not suggest the golden product is the distinguished choice.

Seek an independent outside reading of Theorem 14, for example a short note to a journal in the history of mathematics or in computational geometry. Outside reception, not self-citation, is what would move notability above a specialist audience.
Once read, cite Pustynski's 2014 pages precisely; also read and cite Tahta 1992 and Kulaichev's Addition, or keep listing them as unread with the reason.
